title: Why Mainaka helped
hookLine: once, the story goes, mountains had wings, and one of them owes its wings to Hanuman's father; the Hindu idea of debts carried across generations
carry: rina: a debt of kindness comes due

cards: Sometimes a stranger is kind to you, and later you find out why. Your grandmother taught their mother to read. Your dad once pulled their car out of a ditch in the snow.
The kindness was a thank-you that had waited years for someone from your family to come along. When Mainaka rises from the sea, the Ocean has one reason to help. Mainaka, it turns out, has his own.

teach.b: Mainaka tells Hanuman a story from the earliest age of the world. In those days, he says, the mountains had wings.

They flew wherever they pleased, and the sages and creatures below lived in fear one would come down on them. So Indra, king of the gods, took up his thunderbolt and cut off their wings one after another.

teach.h: INDRA CUTS THEM; VAYU SAVES MAINAKA.
teach.b: When Indra came for Mainaka, the wind god Vayu swept him out of reach and dropped him safely into the ocean, wings and all. Vayu, Mainaka reminds Hanuman, is your father. So I owe you.
Helping you is how I pay your father back. Hold that next to yesterday. The Ocean helps because of Rama's ancestors; Mainaka helps because of Hanuman's father.
Two old debts, coming due on the same crossing. Hindu teaching has a word for this: rina, debt.
Old Vedic texts say every person is born owing three: to the gods, to the sages who handed down knowledge, and to the ancestors, repaid with worship, with study, and with raising a family.
Hindus still honor the last one at shraddha, the offerings made for those who've died. And there's a last turn.

Indra, the very god who cut the mountains' wings, is pleased at what Mainaka has done for Rama's messenger, and grants him safety. That's karma, the teaching that actions bear fruit, told not as a law but as a scene.
A breath of wind long ago means a resting place today.

how: The story of the winged mountains and Indra's thunderbolt is told in several Hindu texts, and the idea of debts to the gods, the sages and the ancestors is still taught, especially when families make shraddha offerings for their dead.

o: the mountain Hanuman lifts and carries to the battle
the mountain the wind god saved from Indra's thunderbolt
the mountain where Hanuman was born to Anjana

games.q: the winged mountain — tap the pairs.
p: carried Mainaka to safety in the sea
repays Vayu by helping his son

s: in this story, mountains once had wings
they flew freely until Indra cut their wings with his thunderbolt.
Indra punishes Mainaka for helping Hanuman
Indra is pleased and grants Mainaka safety.
in Vedic teaching, a person is born owing three debts
to the gods, the sages and the ancestors: rina.

games.q: your dad's old friend won't take money for helping you, because your dad helped him years ago. by today's story, what is that?
o: rina: an old debt of kindness, repaid to the next in the family.
a coincidence; kindness doesn't carry over.
a trade he'd been waiting to collect on.
games.why: Mainaka helped Vayu's son because Vayu once saved him. in Hindu teaching, debts of kindness carry across generations, and they get repaid.

practice: Fold your hands and remember one elder, living or gone, whose kindness you're still living on. Many Hindus say their ancestors' names in prayer; if your family does, say one now.
If you don't pray, just say thank you, silently, by name. Then think of one kindness you could do that might not be repaid for years. Let both rest together as you breathe.

wordCard.voice: Mainaka. The winged mountain the wind god saved from Indra's thunderbolt, who repays the debt by helping Vayu's son, and is granted safety by Indra himself.

orig.note: Sanskrit vāyu, wind, and the wind god: Hanuman's father, who saved Mainaka.

carryVoice: Your line: rina, a debt of kindness comes due. Next comes a meeting that is a test. Rest well.
